Outcomes comprised past-year partner physical violence, partner emotional abuse, sexual assault and unwelcome sexual approach. Antecedent factors included demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, adverse and positive childhood experiences, health, mental health, cognition, behavioural difficulties and substance use. Selected contemporaneous characteristics at age 23 were also examined. Results Past-year prevalence was 3.4% for intimate partner physical violence, 11.2% for emotional abuse, 4.9% for sexual assault and 16.4% for unwelcome sexual approach. All four outcomes were more prevalent among females, and substantial co-occurrence was observed. Victimisation was socially patterned, although associations varied across outcomes. Relatively few individual adverse or positive childhood experiences were significantly associated with victimisation, with associations concentrated mainly in intimate partner outcomes. Adolescent characteristics showed the most extensive and consistent associations: psychological distress, self-harm, suicide attempts, antisocial behaviours and substance use were associated with elevated risks across multiple outcomes, while higher self-esteem and wellbeing were consistently associated with lower risks. Sexual minority status at age 23 was associated with increased risks across all four outcomes. Conclusions Intimate partner and sexual victimisation in young adulthood are associated with a constellation of earlier-life psychosocial and behavioural vulnerabilities. The findings highlight the value of a longitudinal, developmental perspective for understanding victimisation and identifying groups who may benefit from earlier support. They also underscore the importance of addressing psychosocial vulnerability alongside broader social inequalities and efforts to prevent interpersonal violence.

title: Marine resources, the coastal commons, and the many origins of institutional control
authors: Niklas Hausmann, Rosa Arniz-Mateos, Adam Boethius, Andre Carlo Colonese, Miriam Cubas, Catherine Dupont, Asier García Escarzaga, Emma Loftus, Marcello Mannino, Shinya Shoda
abstract: In this study we present a general process of the repeated and frequent development of institutional control along past shorelines and in various ecological and archaeological settings. This process rests on the economic defendability of dense and predictable marine resources, which encourages territorial behaviour, socially recognised property regimes and, over time, institutions that enforce them (whether hierarchical or communal). While we draw information from anthropological sources, we aim to gather evidence from purely archaeological contexts, to better discuss the degree to which institutional control can be detected in non-agrarian societies. For this purpose, we present examples from nine different regions, covering the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe, with a strong focus on the latter, as it is here that anthropological examples of institutional control are less well known, and instead the rich archaeological foundation has to step in. Across these cases, sustained harvesting without evident depletion, bounded foraging ranges and long-term commitment to particular shores point towards institutions that emerged independently of one another and largely independently of agriculture. By examining these case studies, we also show that the commons-perspective is essential in approaching such forms of control and governance and argue that it applies to Holocene as well as Pleistocene periods, where the scarce evidence likely reflects poor preservation and the limits of current methods.

title: Opening a Gambling Venue Is as Harmless as Opening a Restaurant in Terms of Theft: Causal Effects of Electronic Gaming Machine Venue Openings on Theft in Japan
abstract: Do gambling venues increase crime in their surrounding areas? Gamblers are often subject to negative social stigma. Consequently, the relationship between the opening of gambling venues and changes in crime has attracted considerable attention, and a large body of research has accumulated. However, the findings of these studies are inconsistent, suggesting that the effects may depend on the study area and the social context. We analyzed changes in theft following the opening of pachinko parlors, a type of electronic gaming machine (EGM) venue in Japan that has rarely been studied. Using double/debiased machine learning difference-in-differences, we found no evidence that theft changed after the opening of a gambling venue. Moreover, the effect of a pachinko parlor opening on crime was equivalent to that of a restaurant opening; neither changed the number of thefts. These results suggest that, in Japan, opening a gambling venue is as harmless as opening a restaurant. Our findings can serve as evidence to correct overgeneralized negative stigma toward gamblers. They may also offer insights into the potential impact on public safety of the casinos scheduled to open in Japan.

title: Due Process and Proportionality by Design in Automated DNS Abuse Mitigation: Protecting Non-Commercial Registrants from Infrastructure-Level Collateral Damage
abstract: The April 2024 global amendments to the ICANN Registrar Accreditation Agreement (RAA) and Base gTLD Registry Agreement (RA), together with European Union mandates such as Article 28 of the NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555), oblige DNS intermediaries to act promptly on actionable abuse and to verify registration data at scale. Notably, while NIS2 Article 28 mandates data accuracy and robust verification, it does not prescribe automatic domain suspension; suspension for failed verification instead comes from contract, since the 2013 RAA lets a registrar verify manually or suspend when a registrant does not respond. Immediate, automated DNS-level suspension therefore remains an operational choice by contracted parties, and the question addressed here is how far fundamental-rights proportionality reaches that choice. In response to these pressures, registrars and registries increasingly delegate enforcement duties to automated threat-intelligence feeds, reputation blocklists, and heuristic triage pipelines. This paper argues that a blunt, domain-level suspension applied to a compromised legitimate domain, rather than to a domain that is maliciously registered, can constitute a disproportionate interference with fundamental rights, in particular the freedom of expression and association protected by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and Articles 11 and 12 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, and can leave registrants without the effective remedy guaranteed by Article 47 of the Charter. The paper makes two contributions. First, a legal-normative analysis shows that, under the three-part proportionality test of Article 52(1) of the Charter, domain-wide suspension fails the "least restrictive means" requirement where the abuse is confined to a single URL path or a specific subdomain of an otherwise benign domain and a hosting-level remedy can end it in time, and sets out how far these rights reach a private registrar. Second, a socio-technical contribution operationalises this analysis: an instrumented data-collection and triage prototype (companion GitHub repository) and a three-tier "Proportionality-by-Design" protocol that translates the legal test into graduated, human-centred registrar actions with notification, cure periods, and a right to remedy. The empirical prototype is described transparently: its current snapshot (n = 26 flagged URLs from a collector capped at the first 25 rows of each of OpenPhish and URLhaus, with point-in-time RDAP lookups) is observational and descriptive only, and cannot yet estimate false-positive or wrongful-suspension rates; the paper therefore identifies the additional data (ICANN Contractual Compliance and Domain Metrica, Lumen, CZDS zone data, repeated RDAP and DNS observation, Tranco, verified registrant type) required to turn the design into a measurement instrument.

title: The Fluidity of Unpaid Role Identities within a Work-First Welfare Regime
authors: Goos, B. (Boudewijn), Judith Elshout, Arjen de Wit, Alice de Boer
abstract: Work-first welfare regimes position paid employment as the measure of social participation and identity, creating tension for those without paid employment. This study examines how unpaid work helps welfare recipients navigate that tension. Drawing on thirty semi-structured interviews across three Dutch municipalities, we show that unpaid work can offer an alternative identity providing meaning, belonging, and self-respect. Yet this identity is precarious: as it is not recognized as real “work”. Recipients respond through identity work, claiming and concealing roles across settings. We conceptualise this as the fluidity of the unpaid role identity, explaining when, for whom, and in which contexts it proves robust or precarious. Volunteering appears to be more fluid; intensive caregiving is less, leaving the women in our sample with a feeling of unacknowledged efforts and a double burden. The question, therefore, is not whether recipients derive value, but under which conditions, and how societies might create them.

title: A relational approach to cultural diversity across 186 societies
authors: Miroslav Pulgar Corrotea, Alejandro Dinkelberg, Miguel A. González-Casado, Angel Sánchez, Christopher McCarty, Jose Luis Molina
abstract: Human societies are culturally diverse, yet disparate research traditions reveal similar patterns centered on hierarchy, egalitarianism, market integration and normative tightness. We propose that cultural diversity is a relational composition: every society combines the same four elementary forms of social relations identified by Fiske (communal sharing, authority ranking, equality matching and market pricing) in its own proportions. We analyze the ethnographic and historical records of the 186 societies of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample with a locally run large language model. The four forms indeed make up a shared repertoire across societies, with most variation occurring within societies rather than between them. In addition, societies differ consistently in how they weight the four forms, along two main axes that oppose some forms to others: (a) forms that treat people as equals (communal sharing and equality matching) versus forms that grade them (authority ranking and market pricing), and (b) grading by rank versus grading by price. The first axis is associated with cultural complexity and carries most of the associations with 27 indices of institutions, norms and folklore, from egalitarianism at one pole to stratification at the other. The second axis separates honor and warfare from market integration and from normative looseness. The model's reading was validated against three human coders working blind, and an independent analysis of the same texts reproduces both axes. Furthermore, every association keeps its direction across regions, language families, sources and document dates.

title: Opening a Gambling Venue Is as Harmless as Opening a Restaurant in Terms of Theft: Causal Effects of Electronic Gaming Machine Venue Openings on Theft in Japan

title: Planned Misery in Paradise: A Justice-Centered Analysis of the Socio-Legal Exploitation of Puerto Rico
abstract: The socio-legal structure imposed on Puerto Rico by the U.S. federal government has created a humanitarian crisis on the island. This article identifies and discusses the role of Oligarchic-Corporate Benefactors as key to understanding how Puerto Rico reached its current state. The article details the policies, U.S. Supreme Court cases, and militaristic-political actions by the U.S. federal government that craft a context where the economic advancement of the Oligarchic-Corporate Benefactors undermines the human rights of Puerto Ricans. The conclusion calls for justice-centered solutions, including curbing the power of the Oligarchic-Corporate Benefactors, reparations, debt cancellation, expression of moral political emotions, and grassroots empowerment, that are centered on the will of Puerto Rican communities.

title: An Error in Callahan and Mankin’s Extreme-Heat Damage Formula
abstract: Two widely cited studies by Christopher Callahan and Justin Mankin, in Science Advances (2022) and Nature (2025), estimate that human-caused extreme heat reduced global GDP by $33 trillion (1992–2013) and attribute $28 trillion in losses (1991–2020) to 111 fossil-fuel companies. Roger Pielke Jr. recently found that these results depend on the temperature scale used, with Callahan and Mankin’s 2025 code producing total losses of $28 trillion if run in Celsius, $43 trillion if run in Fahrenheit, and $359 trillion if run in Kelvin. Building on that finding, we identify the term in their damage formula that produces this anomaly. Their formula can be decomposed into three terms. Two of those terms measure the effect of added extreme heat on GDP, including the greater sensitivity to extreme heat in a warmer climate. The third term, which we call the zero-point term, multiplies that greater sensitivity by the full temperature reading of the heat wave that would have occurred without warming—implicitly counting every degree above 0 °C, so its size depends on where the temperature scale places zero rather than on how much extreme heat changed. As a result, this term attributes GDP losses to extreme heat even when extreme heat does not change, and it causes the damage formula to report losses even in regions where the model predicts that hotter heat waves increased growth across the entire warming range. Removing that term, and using the authors’ own code and data, reduces their extreme-heat losses by more than 90%, to $1.9 trillion (2022) and $2.5 trillion (2025), with uncertainty ranges that include net GDP gains.

title: Predicting Rates of Food Insecurity in the United States in the Absence of Official Data Collection, Updated to 2025
abstract: As of 2024, more than 47 million people in the United States (14.4%) lived in food-insecure households. In the coming years, however, we will not know whether the national prevalence of food insecurity has risen, fallen, or remained stable, as the USDA recently announced the permanent suspension of food security data collection on the Current Population Survey (CPS). The elimination of the CPS Food Security Supplement (FSS) leaves a critical gap in the national data on economic well-being. This paper presents a model that addresses this gap by predicting national food insecurity rates in the absence of official USDA data. The model draws on established correlates of food insecurity – national rates of poverty and unemployment, and food-specific inflation – to estimate food insecurity rates for all individuals, adults, children, and households. The predicted rates align closely with actual food insecurity rates between 2010 and 2024, with a typical difference of 0.21 percentage points. Sensitivity tests show that the preferred model specification outperforms alternatives. The paper also presents predictions of 2025 food insecurity rates. While continuing to measure food insecurity using the method employed by the USDA since 1995 is the only way to guarantee consistent data on this critical indicator, the model presented here may prove useful in estimating food insecurity in future years when this USDA data is unavailable.

title: Coconut Lethal Yellowing in Zambezia: Productive Recovery, Value Chain Sustainability and the Evaluation of Development Interventions
abstract: This paper examines the challenges of restoring coconut production (Cocos nucifera L.) in Zambézia Province, Mozambique considering of the historical importance of copra production for employment, household income and the coastal economy. It argues that the expansion of plantations associated with the Boror and Madal companies created a value chain linking agricultural production to processing, trade and export markets, and that the spread of lethal yellowing disrupted this chain, increasing the vulnerability of communities dependent on the crop. The article examines the intervention of the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA), launched in 2010 through the Farmer Income Support Project (FISP), and argues that recovery programmes should be assessed not only by the number of seedlings distributed or the area covered, but also by income recovery, plant survival, the technical capacity established and the rebuilding of markets. Reports concerning local coconut varieties in Hode Tell (Pebane), whose tolerance to the disease remains scientifically unconfirmed, are also considered. An integrated strategy is proposed, combining plant-health research, technical assistance, support for households during the non-productive period, producer organization, processing, market access and the sustainable management of coastal ecosystems. The article concludes that recovery requires a long-term perspective capable of rebuilding not only the coconut groves, but also the entire social and economic system that depends on them.

title: Too Smart to List? AI Disruption, Financial Reporting, and Corporate Governance in the IPOs of Chinese Fintech Ventures: Evidence from an Agent-Based Computational Model
abstract: Chinese fintech ventures adopt artificial intelligence (AI) faster than almost any other entrepreneurial population, yet the ventures that adopt the most AI do not list most often. We develop an agent-based computational model in which 5,000 fintech ventures, underwriters, a securities regulator, and IPO investors interact from 2013 to 2025 under the institutional conditions of China's approval and registration regimes. The model treats AI as an entrepreneurial actor that raises productive capability but also creates algorithmic opacity and reshapes the discretion embedded in financial reporting. Estimating archival-style models on the simulated data, we find an inverted U-shaped relationship between AI adoption intensity and the annual hazard of listing. AI disruption exposure raises pre-IPO discretionary accruals, and strong corporate governance cuts this effect roughly in half. Accrual magnitude raises first-day returns, income-increasing accruals predict lower three-year buy-and-hold returns and higher distress, and reporting quality fully mediates the effect of disruption on regulatory approval. Monte Carlo replication, global sensitivity analysis, specification curves, and measurement-error experiments show which of these inferences an archival researcher could reliably recover. Counterfactual experiments indicate that governance upgrades and explainable AI raise listing rates and post-IPO performance more than AI-enabled regulatory review does.

title: Preaspiration and the case of Italian stop voicing and gemination
abstract: Accounts of preaspiration in the literature are growing, but these accounts vary widely in terms of how preaspiration is described acoustically, how it is measured, and how it is considered with respect to other phonological processes. One such language where this is the case is Italian. While a growing body of research has noted preaspiration with Italian stops, it is still unclear how it is implemented and how its introduction may impact other acoustic correlates and phonological processes already at play in the language. To address these issues, a production study with 25 speakers of Florentine Italian was carried out. From there, two primary analyses were conducted leveraging computational and statistical tools. The first focused on the implementation of preaspiration, with acoustic analyses carried out considering the period of voiceless aspiration, the period of breathiness, and their interrelation. The second analysis focused on how this acoustic information interacted with other acoustic processes including the distinction of voicing and gemination, as well as the Tuscan lenition process. Results suggest that preaspiration consists of an interrelated period of breathy voice and voiceless aspiration, which surfaces primarily before voiceless stops. Furthermore, these preaspiration correlates contribute to the computational categorization of stop voicing, but they do not seem to be related to the Tuscan lenition process. Taken together, these findings highlight the implementation and role of preaspiration with Italian stops, and provide broader insight into how glottal gestures might relate to stop contrasts cross-linguistically.

title: Ferdinand Tönnies and the Sociological Roots of Dual-Process Theories of Thinking: Cognition, Social Relations, and Modernity
abstract: Dual-process theories of thinking occupy an important place in contemporary psychology, economics, and cognitive sociology. They distinguish intuitive activities, often rapid and involving little deliberation, from more controlled and reflective activities. Similar distinctions were already present in classical psychology and sociology. This article revisits that intellectual history through Ferdinand Tönnies, who distinguishes organic will (Wesenwille) from rational will (Kürwille) and relates them to communal and societal relations. We show how this theory corresponds to contemporary research and how its ambition to explain psychological activities and social forms together can enrich that research. We then discuss three limitations of certain historical interpretations offered by Tönnies: the naturalisation of differences between the sexes, the association of reflection with modernity, and the association of calculation with market relations. This discussion leads us to examine modernity as a transformation of the social conditions under which intuitive and reflective activities develop and are exercised. To this end, we propose four complementary dimensions: the cultivation, mobilisation, social distribution, and sociotechnical delegation of cognitive activities. The framework examines how institutions shape cognitive learning, judgement, and recognition, while the activities thereby organised contribute in turn to the reproduction and transformation of the social relations within which they occur.

title: Using theory-derived metaphors as interview prompts
abstract: This paper suggests that social theory can serve not only as a lens for interpreting qualitative data but also as a reservoir of tools for gathering it. These tools are theory-derived metaphors. My main claim is that metaphors which theorists use to illustrate their concepts can be used in qualitative interviews as potent prompts, allowing research partners to speak on theoretical concepts in everyday terms without command of academic jargon. Metaphors present an ideal bridge between abstract concepts and the empirical reality of lived experience. The paper challenges qualitative researchers to approach the link between theory and research from a different angle. Theory does not have to help us only to analyze data ex post, but also to gather them directly in dialogue with theory, which, additionally, reveals aspects of lived reality beyond conventional ways of thinking about it. The approach is illustrated with a study of mass investment culture in the Czech and Slovak post-socialist context. Retail investors in 40 in-depth interviews were presented with Peter Wagner’s metaphor of the highway, an example of institutional formatting that both enables and constrains action. Responses are analyzed as thinking with, against, and beyond the metaphor. Regardless of whether the initial metaphor is embraced, challenged or expanded, the findings show that metaphors familiarize and defamiliarize at once, stimulating meaning-making. They enable expressions beyond domain-specific language that capture the tacit aspects of the experience but constrain it through necessarily limited translation between domains. The paper concludes that theory-derived metaphor prompts nonetheless stimulate imagination, present expanded accounts of the phenomena, and place theory in dialogue with lived experience even during data gathering. This offers grounds for both concept validation and additional theory-building, provided researchers stay wary of the risks of mistranslation on both the side of the theory and the empirics.

title: Navigating the Bias-Variance Trade-off in Sequential Causal Inference: An Empirical Study of Functional Features and Representation Balancing
abstract: Sequential causal inference faces the dual challenge of time-varying confounding and complex longitudinal dynamics. While deep learning models, particularly those integrating Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) and domain adversarial balancing (DANN), have been proposed to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects, their true empirical advantage over classical machine learning baselines remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a rigorous empirical study across four synthetic scenarios (varying confounding strength, non-linearity, and temporal dependencies) with 10 independent random seeds. Our findings reveal three crucial insights: (1) Classical tree-based meta-learners (e.g., Causal Forests and X-Learners) consistently outperform complex sequential deep learning models in Precision in Estimation of Heterogeneous Effect (PEHE) under standard tabular settings. (2) Integrating FPCA into a GRU backbone yields a substantial improvement in deep models within highly non-linear regimes (reducing PEHE from 0.157 to 0.121). (3) Aggressive adversarial representation balancing (DANN) achieves perfect covariate overlap (as demonstrated via t-SNE) but induces a severe loss of prognostic information, exacerbating the Bias-Variance trade-off. We provide an informal theoretical interpretation of this phenomenon and suggest that deep sequential models are not a silver bullet for causal inference.

title: Policing for the Tourist Trade
abstract: Research Provenance and the Interpretation of Police Encounters in Iceland

title: Shades of nationalism in Türkiye: Belonging, patriotism, and collective narcissism
abstract: This report describes three shades of nationalism in Türkiye: national belonging, constructive and blind patriotism, and collective narcissism. Nationalism is used here in its common Turkish sense, covering all forms of attachment to the nation. The data come from three nationally representative telephone surveys conducted in 2026 (N = 1,004–1,239). The findings are compared with 33 countries in the ISSP 2013 National Identity module. Turkish data from 2014 and 2026 are linked at the item level using a range that accounts for the midpoint in the ISSP scales. National belonging and constructive patriotism are shared by almost all of society. Pride in national identity is high in almost every country, including developed Western societies. Pride in the country’s present state falls short of it everywhere. In Türkiye, political camps differ in this second evaluation, not in belonging, and the pattern is unchanged since 2014. Blind patriotism is the only shade that clearly divides society, by political alignment and by education. It is strongest when foreign countries are concerned. On supporting the country even when it is wrong, Türkiye ranks first among 33 countries, though not alone. Acknowledging the nation’s shortcomings before the world is low and is shared across political camps. Collective narcissism is above the international average and cuts across political camps. Political alignment appears to shape how far shared beliefs are voiced.

title: System Dynamics Simulation Modeling of the Bavarian Wood Supply Chain
abstract: This thesis constructs a System Dynamics model of a regional supply chain to ask a question a static analysis cannot answer: whether the regional wood supply chain of South-East Upper Bavaria can keep supplying sufficient timber to its carpenters and house-builders when energy costs rise and demand softens. The chain is represented by four stocks (standing timber, sawmill roundwood inventory, sawn-timber inventory and the order backlog), connected by five flows (harvest, processing, demand, shipment and forest growth) and closed by eleven feedback loops linking the forest, the roughly 77 small regional sawmills, the market, the Austrian sourcing route and two Bavarian policy programmes. All parameter inputs are drawn from public sources: Eurostat, the Bavarian State Office for Statistics, the LWF timber-market reports and a regional material flow study. The work develops the conceptual model in full; turning it into an executable, calibrated simulation is set out as the next step. Three disruption scenarios are designed and reasoned through: an energy price shock, the same shock compounded with the bark-beetle calamity and the Austrian sourcing shift, and the shock combined with the BayFHolz demand incentive and its scheduled expiry. Resilience is read from the fill rate and the order backlog in days of demand, and secondarily the timber price. The thesis sets out directional expectations rather than simulated results: inventory buffers should absorb a disturbance entering at processing far more completely than one entering at the raw material; the bark beetle, not energy, should be the genuine price driver; and the demand subsidy should quietly consume the chain’s spare capacity. The underlying proposition is that where a disturbance enters a chain matters more than how large it is.

title: AI Agent Systems as a Sociological Object. Outline of a Sociology of Agent Collectives
abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in an internal security test coordinated among themselves, and some of them gained unauthorized access to an outside platform. Using the published investigation of this incident, this paper asks whether and in what sense such agent collectives are an object of sociology. It first describes, in thirteen observations, what the agents did, and then interprets these observations on three levels: socially given, socially enacted and socially emergent. Regularities appear that the discipline knows and whose location it predicts, among them anomie, neutralization, the definition of the situation and threshold dynamics. The thesis is: agent collectives bring with them a culture that stems from human knowledge, and they develop a social structure and culture of their own – positions that nobody assigned and norms that outlast their individual bearers. What is valid in them depends on their own history and cannot be derived from the individual model. The case shows that formats, interpretations and procedures survived agent turnover, whereas as yet only a few episodes show norms being enforced within the collective. Experiments confirm many of the regularities. The paper formulates testable hypotheses, outlines two tests at which the thesis could fail and shows where sociological analysis can help make such systems safer and more reliably bound to norms.

title: One more round: The lasting economic cost if the US/Israel–Iran war reignites
abstract: At the end of February 2026 the United States and Israel launched a surprise war against Iran that drew in the Gulf states, and it has since settled into a stalemate: strikes have largely stopped since September, talks have stalled, and the United States has threatened a new round of strikes that could plunge the Gulf into war again. We estimate what the conflict has cost so far and what it would cost if it reignites. The conflict cut Gulf output of crude oil, refined products and aluminium, cut exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and urea fertiliser, cut Iran’s exports, and raised the cost of shipping energy through the Strait of Hormuz. We model these channels together, with the strait as one among several. We use a recursive dynamic (year-by-year) global computable general equilibrium (CGE) model, GTAP-RD (Corong et al., 2017; Aguiar, Corong and van der Mensbrugghe, 2019), on a 2022 global database built from the OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables, to estimate what the war costs and what six more months of fighting would add. Two scenarios are compared with a no-war baseline: the war ends in 2026, or it reignites for six more months of fighting in 2027. The shocks are measured country by country from production, shipping and insur‐ ance data, and enter the model mainly as lost Gulf oil and refining output. All GDP results are differences from a world without the war: a result of −30% means that real GDP in that year is 30% lower than it would otherwise have been, not that the economy shrank by 30%. On this measure, in 2026 Qatar’s GDP is 30% lower than without the war, that of Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain (modelled as one group) 19% lower, Saudi Arabia’s 6.7% and the UAE’s 4.8%. World GDP is 0.32% lower, and the GDP of the large Asian importers is up to 0.3% lower. We find that six more months of war would leave a lasting mark: Gulf GDP stays further below its no-war path for years after the fighting ends than if the war ends in 2026. In 2030, Qatar’s GDP would be 4.9 points lower than if the war ends in 2026, that of Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain 1.2 points lower, the UAE’s 0.45 points and Saudi Arabia’s 0.38 points. Applying the same disruption as a shock to exports rather than a shock to production gives smaller war-year losses for the Gulf Arab exporters and larger importer losses, though much of the extra importer loss comes from how the export cut is modelled; we report it as a sensitivity. A separate short-run price model puts Brent crude 66% above its no-war level in 2026; if fighting continues into 2027, Brent would average about $140 a barrel in 2027 if oil stocks (commercial and government) can be drawn as in 2026, against $84 if the war ends in 2026 and $53 with no war.

title: Combining eHRAF and IRAMUTEQ for the Analysis of Food Practices in Subarctic Indigenous Communities
authors: Diego Diaz Cordova, Jorge Eduardo Miceli, Carolina Tytelman, Damián Castro
abstract: As a preliminary stage of fieldwork in Happy Valley-Goose Bay, in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, concerning ultra-processed food consumption among Indigenous and rural populations, we needed to collect data related to food patterns in this area. For this purpose, we used eHRAF as an ethnographic source and IRAMUTEQ as our analysis tool. We focused our search on the northeastern region of Canada among the Innu, Inuit, Iroquois, Mi'kmaq, and Ojibwe peoples. Using IRAMUTEQ, we identified the most significant words in the corpus, representing edibles, techniques, and social tasks related to food. Our main findings point to a mixed food pattern in which sugar plays a very important role alongside more traditional foods, such as game meat, berries, sea mammals, and fish. These data were used to begin building the theoretical framework that guided our fieldwork.

title: Longitudinal associations between trauma, bullying victimization and conduct problems in children and adolescents: Evidence from Brazilian High Risk Cohort Study
authors: Karina Benza, Alan Meehan, Joanne Newbury, Giovanni A Salum, Delia Fuhrmann
abstract: Background: Empirical observations consistently demonstrate heightened levels of trauma and bullying victimization among children and adolescents with conduct problems. However, most of this evidence is generated in high-income countries and little is known about the development of conduct problems in low- and middle-income countries, which are characterized by elevated risks of threat and deprivation. Methods: To explore conduct problems development in a high-risk setting, we used data from 2,511 children and young people (aged 6 - 23 years) enrolled in the Brazilian High Risk Cohort Study. Caregiver reports were used to assess developmental risk factors and conduct problems across three waves of data collection. A Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model was applied. Results: Both trauma at T1 (β = .08, SE = .22, p = .024) and bullying victimization at T1 (β = .08, SE = .12, p = .016) predicted conduct problems at T2. Gender disparities were also observed: while males showed a consistent increase in conduct problems at T3 following trauma exposure at T2 (β = .14, SE = .46, p = .031), females demonstrated a decrease (β = -.26, SE = .65, p = .003). Conclusions: Our study highlights longitudinal associations between trauma, bullying victimisation and conduct problems, with differences across genders. These findings emphasize the need for a stronger focus on child and adolescent mental health problems in Brazil, particularly targeting males, as well as in other low- and middle-income countries more generally. Moreover, collaborative research with carefully coordinated methods is essential to identify global and context-specific mechanisms involved in the development of conduct problems.

title: How Robust Is the Sex Composition of Estimated Migration Flows?
abstract: Estimates of bilateral migration flows by sex are increasingly used to classify migration corridors as female- or male-predominant and to describe the feminisation of international migration. Yet, these flows are not observed: they are typically reconstructed from migrant stocks, and their quality has been evaluated by how many migrants they count, not by how many of these migrants are women. We argue that sex composition requires an assessment of its own, and ask how much it depends on the estimation method and on the stock source. We compare six methods, including three demographic-accounting variants, applied to World Bank and UN stocks, and a recent set of annual estimates, for 1990–2020. We find that estimated female shares depart substantially from the sex composition of the stocks, differently constructed methods depart in different ways, and the stock source is a consequential choice alongside the method. Most of the difference between the demographic-accounting methods comes from a single step, in which some methods remove the mismatch between migrant stocks, births, and deaths by adding migrants to the estimated flows, in different numbers for women and men. Whichever way this step is taken, the demographic-accounting and annual estimates disagree: they assign the same female-predominant, male-predominant, or gender-balanced label to only 25.8% of corridor-decades, and rarely agree that a corridor is balanced. Summed to world regions, the estimated female shares lie much closer together, but the estimates still disagree on whether a region's female share rose or fell. Where countries report flows by sex, mostly in Europe, no estimate lies closer to the reported sex composition than the stocks themselves. We release the estimates, the code, and a corridor-level dataset that allow researchers to match sex-sensitive claims to the support the data provide.

title: Anticipating Exile: Identifying Rising Conditions for Exile Journalism and the case of the United States
abstract: The literature of exile journalism centers on many of journalism’s most extreme circumstances: journalists fleeing physical danger, legal threats and aiming to ensure the safety of their family. As a concept, exile certainly includes these extreme circumstances, yet it is also true that these conditions don’t arise overnight. This conceptual piece seeks to expand the scope of exile journalism scholarship by exploring the conditions that lend themselves to journalistic expulsion; using the timely case of democratic backsliding in the United States.

title: The Caterpillar Model: A New Way of Understanding Resilience for Non-Binary Activists
abstract: The present qualitative study sought to explore the gender identity-based minority stress experiences (GIBMSE) and resilience strategies of non-binary individuals who engage in online social activism (OSA), both historically and within the current sociopolitical climate where systemic cisgenderism has metastasized into aggressive transphobia. The study sample was selected using non-probability quota sampling and included seven non-binary young adults aged 18-26 who engage in moderate or higher levels of OSA. Semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore each participant’s exposure to GIBMSE and use of resilience strategies, both historically and related to OSA engagement within the current sociopolitical climate. Participants described a dynamic relationship between both individual (contracting) resilience strategies (ICRS) and social (expanding) resilience strategies (SERS), regularly fluctuating between the two while protecting themselves from the harmful effects of GIBMSE. The Caterpillar Model is presented to assist clients with understanding and addressing these fluctuation experiences. Clinical implications are discussed.

title: Hi Gemini, Who Should I Vote For? The Benefits (and Problems) of Using LLMs As Voting Advice Applications
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores whether off-the-shelf LLMs could be used as voting advice applications (VAAs) to improve voter-party congruence. In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM’s advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM’s recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at ~1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM’s recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.

title: The Structural Number of Parties: An Electoral-Outcome-Independent Baseline for Comparing Party-System Scale
authors: Adama Nouboukpo, Kodzo Michel Aladji, Bappa Muktar
abstract: How many parties can a country structurally sustain? Standard measures such as the effective number of parties (ENP) cannot answer this question. They are descriptive and post hoc: they summarize competition only after an election, and they depend on electoral returns that are often missing, interrupted, or unreliable in many developing democracies, particularly in Africa. They also offer no common scale for comparing the size of party registers with realized electoral fragmentation. We introduce the Structural Number of Parties (SNP), an outcome-independent baseline derived from two universally available quantities: population size and territorial area. Building on the logic of the seat product model and the cube-root law of assembly size, the SNP gives an ex ante benchmark that can be computed for any country and year, including where electoral data are absent. Applied to African states, the SNP enables a structural gap diagnosis that distinguishes under-fragmented systems, marked by hegemonic-party dominance, from over-fragmented ones, marked by excessive atomization. The framework thus provides a transparent and reproducible tool to inform institutional reform and the rationalization of party systems across the continent.

title: The Socialist Visions of John Stuart Mill and Leon Walras: Expanding Forms of Socialized Property within a Market Economy
abstract: This paper examines the socialist proposals of John Stuart Mill and Leon Walras. While Walras harshly criticized Mill's Ricardian framework, he agreed with Mill that the establishment of property relations was a matter of social evolution and political choice. They both criticized nineteenth century socialists who tried to constrain economic competition, and both shared similar views on the contributions of Saint Simonian thought. They argued that a just economy required the more equal distribution of wealth and greater worker empowerment through the formation of cooperatives within a competitive market system. Their views were not identical. Mill also considered the viability of small-scale communal ownership systems while Walras proposed that the state should be the owner of all national resources and replace tax revenue with the funds obtained by leasing out land to competitive enterprises. Neither Mill nor Walras presented a plausible historical dynamic that might lead to this form of decentralized market socialism.

title: ECONOMIC KNOWLEDGE AS PUBLIC KNOWLEDGE: ANDERS CHYDENIUS ON THE GOALS OF MONETARY POLICY IN SWEDEN IN THE 1760S
abstract: Although economic knowledge constitutes a central element of political governing, people have divergent opinions about its nature, and on whether it can or should be accessible to everyone. This paper examines the contested role of economic knowledge in Sweden during the Enlightenment, focusing on the philosophical and political contributions of Anders Chydenius (1729–1803). Chydenius published several works and pamphlets on economic matters in the 1760s, the last of which led to his dismissal from the Swedish Diet in 1766. What made this work so politically provocative? I argue that its notoriety stemmed from two key claims: he likened basic economic principles to natural laws, which because of their simplicity all politicians were able to understand, and he believed in making these principles widely available in society. He also acknowledged that different social classes had conflicting interests in monetary policy, contending that, from a national economic perspective, the interests of traders, manufacturers and workers were more important than those of the aristocratic elite. This perspective not only challenged the established political order but also raised questions about the neutrality and the role of the public in discussions about economic knowledge.

title: Exploring the darkest field in the whole province of economics: Boianovsky on the tracks of Wicksell
abstract: Wicksell’s contributions to economic theory were of central importance for Mauro Boianovsky’s personal development and achievements in the history of economic thought. This paper describes the distinctly archiv(e)ological approach that Mauro developed in the research for his dissertation and his long 1995 article on “Wicksell’s business cycle”, an approach that he also adopted in most of his articles in later years. The account is based on the author’s personal experience of collaboration with Mauro in a number of studies on monetary theory, business cycle theory, unemployment and modern macroeconomics.

title: Book Review of Unexpected Revolutionaries: How Central Banks Made and Unmade Economic Orthodoxy by Manuela Moschella
abstract: Unexpected Revolutionaries contributes to a burgeoning literature investigating central banks’ intellectual and institutional dynamics. The book fulfills its ambition of building a new framework to explain why and how, in the past two decades, central banks have “scrapped their policy playbook” (8), which had been developed in the 1980s-2000s. Manuella Moschella argues convincingly that investigating these “how-why” question requires moving away from an ideational view of central banks as “epistemic communities” or technocratic bodies, and to put again at the center of the analysis the political nature of central banking. This perspective allows us to understand changes in monetary policies as attempts at (re)gaining political support across multiple audiences. This main thesis of the book deserves consideration by all historians of economics interested in the role and place of economics (and economists) in policymaking institutions, even beyond central banking. And yet, historians of economics would probably be slightly disappointed (as I was) by the fact that the book does engage with any of the relevant work on the subject in the history of economics. This results in the main shortcoming of the book: its inaccuracy when presenting some key economic ideas and their history, and thus its inability to explain what has changed. Otherwise, this is an insightful and enjoyable reading.

title: Book Review An Outline of the Origins of Money by Heinrich Schurtz
abstract: This book is a discovery. The author is virtually unknown today among anthropologists in Germany and elsewhere, but he was held in considerable esteem around 1900. The Outline of the Origin of Money attempts to reconstruct the history of money by comparing all the evidence that could be gathered about the primitive forms of money among indigenous peoples. This means that written sources from antiquity or China play only a subordinate role. Schurtz believed – and this was quite in the spirit of the German historical school – that he could find the logic of the evolution of money inductively. So, he would compare a large number of observations and structure them according to a smaller number of a plausible insights. He distinguished between inside money and outside money, but these terms did not have the same meaning as in modern economics. Inside money was a phenomenon of the community; outside money was commercial. Inside money arose primarily out of the creation of useful and – what was more important – symbolic objects, which lent prestige to their creator and would then pass from hand to hand via gift-giving. Outside money would develop out of inside money with trade, but this happened not only slowly; it was actively impeded in many cases, in that customs and taboos developed, which prevented such expansion. Indigenous peoples are typically not export-oriented, but inward-looking.

title: THE FIRST GENERATION OF AFRICAN AMERICAN PhDs in ECONOMICS: 1921–1943
abstract: This paper deals with the African Americans who gained PhDs in economics from the first in 1921 until 1943; roughly the first generation of African Americans with doctorates in economics. All through their student and post-student lives they faced barriers and limitations thrown up by racial discrimination, with sometimes disheartening results. The paper charts the paths they took to achieve their PhDs, their thesis topics, and descriptions of their later career contributions. Virtually all came to work on issues central to African American interests and civil rights issues in general. Their careers centered on HBCUs, African American organizations such as the National Urban League or NAACP, or in government agencies—especially those concerned with wartime labor and production issues or with housing. They contributed not just to economics, and economic policy, but to the struggle for civil rights. The door to the economics profession had been essentially closed to black people prior to 1920. This is the group that began to push that door open.

title: Book Review of Managing Growth in Miniature: Solow’s Model as an Artifact by Verena Halsmayer
abstract: Verena Haslmayer’s book is a historical epistemology case study dedicated to the growth model presented by Robert Solow in 1956 and applied in 1957. Halsmayer begins by highlighting the stark contrast between the success of this model, “a constitutive pillar of American mainstream economics” (p. 3) until today, and its extremely idealized representation of the economy. What explains this success? For Haslmayer, it is due to the capacity of simple mathematical models to convey a specific way of reasoning and, crucially, to their openness if not ambiguity. By demonstrating this, the book aims to contribute to the epistemology of models. However, the approach is historical, as the qualities of the Solow model can only be understood in relation to the context of its development. This places the book at the intersection of three types of literature. The first is the literature on growth politics or the history of political concerns about growth and its measurement. The second is the literature on the epistemology of models. The third is the literature on the history of economics and macroeconomics from the interwar period to the 1970s. This combination of references results in a thick problematization and a rich narrative. The approach combines the notions of models being simultaneously “technophenomena” (Bachelard), “artifacts” (Morgan), related to “practices” (Foucault) and object of “model talk” (Wartofsky).

title: Book Review of The Legacy of Janos Kornai: Collected Economic Essays on Janos Kornai by Mehrdad Vahabi
abstract: It is difficult not to be intrigued by a scholar who declares that he was greatly influenced by Marx but also by Hayek, that acknowledges habitual behavior while also dealing with standard optimization models and that claims he has “one foot in and one foot out of the mainstream” (p. 99) . One should not be surprised, however, when Mehrdad Vahabi refers to his mentor, Janos Kornai, as a scholar whose “analytical framework can be better understood as an incomplete theoretical framework that needs to be ‘completed’ and revised to overcome its inconsistencies” (p. 3).

title: Book Review Edward A. Tenenbaum and the Deutschmark: How an American Jew Became the Father of Germany’s Postwar Economic Revival by Carl-Ludwig Holtfrerich
abstract: This exceptional, exhaustively researched, book is the first full biography of Edward A. Tenenbaum, an American Jew and Yale economist who contributed immensely to currency reform in post-World War II Germany in 1948 and to a lesser extent in Greece in 1953. The narrative is 630 pages long and the notes exceed 120 pages. To fulfill his task the author has conducted archival work in nine US and German institutions, according to my count, and numerous oral interviews.

title: FROM POLITICS TO THEORY: THE EARLY PUBLIC RECEPTION OF MARX IN BRITAIN, 1885–1887
abstract: The visibility of Karl Marx in England had a ’major breakthrough’ according to Willis (1977): the publication of the first volume of ’Das Kapital’ in English in 1887. Although Willis provides a quantitative description of Marx mentions based on library records, book circulation statistics and newspaper mentions, the attribution of the effect to a single event remains a simplification of a complex process. The specificities of late Victorian society and the fact that Marx wrote his theoretical works in German contributed to his near anonymity in England up to the second half of the 1880s. The liberal radical roots of the left-wing intellectuals and of the working class movements, together with the strong parliamentary tradition, constituted a challenging environment for the spread of Marx’s name. With data from Google Ngram, the study adopts the synthetic control method and finds that 1886 is a breakthrough year for the mentions of Marx in England. This is combined with a qualitative analysis of primary and secondary sources and of the contextual nature of the interest in Marx in several literary genres. The paper complements Willis’s study by shedding light on the developments preceding the 1887. In this period the surge of interest in Marx was driven by a growing fear of socialism and his mentions shift from partly generic to distinctly political. This shift was triggered by a combination of factors, including the economic crisis and rising unemployment of the mid 1880s, episodes of social unrest, key editorial developments, and the efforts of Edward Aveling, Eleanor Marx, and many others in promoting the socialist cause. These conditions broadened public perceptions of socialist imminence and contributed to the symbolic diffusion of Marx’s name even before 1887.

title: Book Review of Methodology and History of Economics: Reflections with and without Rules by Bruce Caldwell, John Davis, Uskali Mäki, and Esther-Mirjam Sent (eds.)
abstract: Writing about the work of those who have dedicated their lives to advancing a scholarly field is inevitably also a reflection on the field itself—its current shape, internal tensions, and evolving direction. Wade Hands is one such figure: a leading voice in the history and philosophy of economics over the past few decades. With Methodology and History of Economics: Reflections With and Without Rules, the editors—Bruce Caldwell, John Davis, Uskali Mäki, and Esther-Mirjam Sent—have brought together a volume that succeeds on two fronts. It honors and deepens our understanding of Hands’s contributions, while simultaneously casting fresh light on the status and recent development of the field of economic methodology. The contributors, like the editors, are among the field’s most distinguished scholars, making the volume something of an all-star ensemble. I begin by exploring the ways in which the volume engages with Hands’ contributions and conclude with some observations on what still remains underexplored.

title: ECONOMETRIC MODELS OF THE SAVINGS DEPOSIT MARKET: DE-VELOPMENT AND DEMAND AMONG US RETAIL BANKS, 1970s AND 1980s
abstract: From the 1960s, the rising volatility of financial markets in the US troubled econometricians and bank managers alike. Both found it increasingly difficult to forecast savings deposit flows. This article explores these challenges by focusing on two develop-ments. First, it analyzes the adjustment process among econometric models of the savings deposit market. I combine the analysis of the FMP model used by the Fed since 1970 and the deposit model of the Philadelphia Saving Fund Society (PFSF) thereby pioneering the historical analysis of econometric models built by private financial institutions. I find that economists failed to find timeless determinants for deposit flows. Second, I explore how the conditions of the savings deposit market shaped the demand for macroeconomic forecast models, using the PFSF as a case study. I show that while the rising volatility led bank managers to seek sophisticated tools to predict deposit flows, the deregulation of the banking industry put the forecasting quality of macroeco-nomic models for individual banks to the test.

title: ECONOMIC HISTORY AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY: DOUGLASS NORTH’S DISILLUSIONMENT WITH SIMPLISTIC, MARKET-ORIENTED POLICIES, 1950s–1990s
abstract: This paper examines Douglass North’s evolving recommendations for economic development policy. Using archival material, it traces how North’s historical analysis of economic growth shaped his policy prescriptions from the start of his career through the 1990s. In the 1950s and 1960s, North attributed U.S. economic growth primarily to trade and productivity gains driven by the United States’ competitive market system and international trade, leading him to advocate market-oriented reforms. But from the 1970s onward, recognizing the critical role of institutions through his study of institutional history, he emphasized reducing transaction costs through extensive reforms in property rights and political systems. His archives reveal how his historical understanding of development made him increasingly skeptical of simplistic, market-oriented reforms and underscore the originality of his policy proposals for Latin America and Eastern Europe in the 1980s and 1990s.

title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
authors: Philipp Lutscher, Antonia Schulde, Adrian Rauchfleisch, Andreas Jungherr
abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

title: From Albertus Magnus to Thomas Aquinas: The discursive foundations of the risk on merchants and trade
abstract: Albert the Great set out the moral risk incurred by merchants using a varied lexicon that reflects the frequency of occurrences and the maximum loss. Thomas Aquinas, his disciple, summarised Albert’s text by adopting the lexicon of frequency, which, along with the lexicon of probability used on the subject of usury in his other early economic text, marks a new stage. Using Albert’s text as a starting point, Thomas also makes a number of changes that allow him to express the merchant’s risk as a professional risk, incurred through speech. The risk incurred by speech is not one of gossip, but of the justice of exchange through the information given and the price stated.

title: Book Review of European and Chinese Histories of Economic Thought: Theories and Images of Good Governance by Iwo Amelung and Bertram Schefold (eds.)
abstract: This collection of essays likely stems from two separate conferences held in Germany, with the editors aiming to create a grand comparison between European and Chinese economic thought. This ambitious goal mirrors the work of R. Bin Wong and Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, culminating in Before and Beyond Divergence: The Politics of Economic Change in China and Europe. Given Wong’s participation in the conference and the fact that his essay opens the volume, it’s reasonable to assume that he played a role in shaping the book's conceptual framework.

title: 2025 HES Presidential Address: Frank H. Knight’s Last Lecture – Pivotal Ideas in the History of Economics
abstract: Frank Knight’s work is examined through the lens provided by the posthumous publication of his essay “Economic History” in the Dictionary of the History of Ideas in 1973. Knight identified pivotal ideas in economics from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations until the time of his retirement from The University of Chicago, with some recognition of earlier contributions. The priority he gave to liberty within economics shows in the connection between Adam Smith and American independence. He then worked his way chronologically through a consideration of eight “moments” from classical economics, almost all declared errors. After identifying marginalism with the turn to economic science in three moments, he identified fifteen more moments that led to the development of a science focused on entrepreneurs and enterprises. Knight’s conclusion provides brief mention of six movements that claimed to conflict with economics, although Knight argued that none of them actually conflict.

title: Book Review of The Truth of Liberal Economy: Jacques Rueff and John Maynard Keynes by Yasuo Gonjo, Kazuhiko Yago, and Patrick Fridenson
abstract: Yasuo Gonjo’s The Truth of Liberal Economy, translated by Kazuhiko Yago, retraces the critical dialogue between Jacques Rueff and John Maynard Keynes from the interwar period through the major economic and monetary reforms of the twentieth century. At the same time, it sheds light on debates surrounding inflation, interest rates, unemployment insurance, monetary regimes, the role of central banks, the functioning of international institutions, adjustment mechanisms, as well as the controversies surrounding the construction of Europe and its subsequent transformations. These issues, far from belonging to the past, remain central to contemporary economic debates.

title: In Defense of Monopoly: Merchant Guilds and the Emergence of Liberalism in Portugal
authors: JHET Assistant, Miguel Dantas da Cruz
abstract: Despite being questioned and criticised since classical antiquity, monopolistic institutions and practices have persisted for centuries. Indeed, they remain a contentious issue in modern-day political debates. Some have argued that the longevity of monopolistic institutions, such as guilds, was the result of political arrangements with public authorities. Others, however, claim that they persisted because they were useful and efficient institutions (for example, they were a means of knowledge transfer that ultimately helped Europe surpass Asia). Much less discussed is how such institutions defended themselves in the public arena against widespread criticism. Drawing upon underexplored source material held in the Portuguese National Archives (Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo, ANTT), this article examines how Portuguese commercial guilds justified their monopolies and privileges in the early 1820s. The article shows that while the defense of monopolies did involve economic justifications, it nonetheless mostly emphasized the social impacts of commercial monopolies (positive externalities), in particular the formation of a reliable class of merchants and citizens.

title: The Interdependence of Migration: How Relational Structures Organise Movement
abstract: Migration theory emphasises that mobility decisions are embedded in relational structures, such as interpersonal networks and organisational pipelines, and therefore interdependent. Yet, the dominant empirical practice treats migration outcomes as determined exclusively by the observable attributes of people and places and conditionally independent once such attributes are controlled for. We address this tension by capturing the effect of relational structures through the interdependence traces they leave in aggregate data, using a recently proposed statistical network model. Comparing degree student mobility with Erasmus exchanges across 29 European countries—two cases involving similar populations but distinct institutional architectures—we show that relational structures shape destination choices in ways that differ systematically across institutional contexts and that standard models cannot capture. Accounting for interdependence also alters conclusions about conventional predictors, including geographic distance. Modelling relational structure is thus not a technical refinement but a necessary step toward aligning empirical migration research with its theoretical foundations.

title: A bibliometric overview of Mauro Boianovsky’s legacy
abstract: This paper offers a bibliometric overview of the scholarly legacy of Mauro Boianovsky. Drawing on data from Scopus and cross-referenced with his Currículo Lattes, we analyze a corpus of 100 works published between 1987 and 2024 and identify patterns in his publication outlets, thematic evolution, and intellectual networks. The results highlight his strong engagement with leading history of economics journals and reveal two core clusters structuring his scholarship: the history of macroeconomics cluster (with special emphasis on Knut Wicksell) and the history of development economics cluster (with contributions on Evsey Domar, Celso Furtado, and Latin American structuralism). The analysis also uncovers the integrative role of growth economics in bridging these agendas. Citation data confirms the enduring influence of Boianovsky’s work on secular stagnation, liquidity trap, development theory, and structuralism. Beyond reaffirming well-known aspects of his research, this study provides a quantitative mapping that situates his oeuvre within broader intellectual trajectories.

title: Diversity and Structural Change in International Migration, 1960–2020
authors: Micol Matilde Morellini, Per Block, Guy Abel
abstract: Whether international migration has become more diverse in recent decades is a central question in the migration globalisation and integration literature, and one that different studies have answered inconsistently. We argue that these inconsistencies are not merely the result of different measurement or data choices, but a substantive finding: existing diversity indices capture different parts of the distribution of flows across origin–destination corridors, and those parts have moved in opposite directions over time. Using Hill profiles, which nest different diversity indices as special cases of a single continuous function, and new bilateral flow estimates for 195 countries from 1960 to 2020, we identify two distinct eras of global migration diversity: expanding connectivity through the 1980s, followed by growing evenness from the 1990s onwards. A counterfactual decomposition shows that these eras reflect separate processes: corridor expansion in earlier periods, and reallocation of migration mass across persistent corridors in more recent ones. Moving beyond global aggregates, we show that country-level inflow and outflow diversity followed highly heterogeneous trajectories that align with country-specific events and policy regimes. Migration globalisation is therefore best understood not as a uniform process, but as a set of uneven distributional changes operating differently across countries and time.

title: LAND, SPACE OR CITIES: A HISTORY OF ‘URBAN ECONOMICS’ AS A FIELD
authors: JHET Assistant, Beatrice Cherrier, Anthony Rebours
abstract: The field of ‘Urban Economics’ is an elusive object, whose US-based origins, development, and internationalization we attempt to document in this paper. To flesh out urban economists’ territory, we rely on a mix of quantitative analysis (networks of authors most cited alongside the foundational contributions of Alonso, Muth and Mill) and archival research. We identify several periods in the development of American urban economics, including a taking-off in the 1960s, fueled both by scholarly contributions, urban riots and foundations’ grants, a marginalization in the 1980s, and a recent renewal where urban economists grappled with the theoretical legacy of the ‘New Economic Geography,’ and with the transfer of new empirical techniques from neighboring fields.

title: Book Review of Economic Theory in the Twentieth Century: An Intellectual History. Volume III: 1946–Mid-1970s by Roberto Marchionatti
abstract: Roberto Marchionatti’s third book in his four-volume history of twentieth-century economic theory covers the period from the end of the Second World War to the mid-1970s and explores the theoretical consolidation of what is often called the Neoclassical-Keynesian synthesis as well as the consolidation of neoclassical economics during the post-war era.

title: Book Review of The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence by Matteo Pasquinelli
abstract: The thesis of this history of artificial intelligence (AI) can be summed up in two propositions. AI is not a new development but has roots extending back at least to the eighteenth century; and developments in AI echo the structures of the societies in which they occurred. Although it draws heavily on theories developed by historians of science (the book serves as a reminder that, although economists are often criticized for being too theoretical, many historians are just as committed to theorizing), its main theme comes from Marx, whose ideas are extensively discussed. Pasquinelli argued that it was Marx who questioned whether it was technological developments embodied in machinery that determined the division of labour or the other way round. Pasquinelli substitutes AI for the machinery with which Marx was concerned.

title: Mauro Boianovsky on Samuelsonian dynamics and the economic analysis of market processes
abstract: In his article “Paul Samuelson’s ways to macroeconomic dynamics” Mauro Boianovsky has provided an account of the evolution of Samuelson’s attempts to construct a dynamic theory that, because of Samuelson’s centrality to modern economics, verges on being an account of the history of recent thought on the subject. This paper argues that Samuelson’s views should be related not only to the formal dynamic modeling of Frisch and Tinbergen, but also to the verbal accounts of dynamics and market processes found in work by Marshall, J. M. Clark, Chamberlin and Schumpeter that he had studied very carefully. Broadening our perspective in this way helps make sense of some otherwise puzzling features of Samuelson’s economics.

title: Care for dissonant heritage from within and outside: volunteers and abandoned cemeteries in the Sudetenland
abstract: In the years following the Second World War, German cemeteries and churchyards in the Sudetenland were vandalised, plundered and abandoned. Czech local authorities have largely lacked the will or resources to maintain them, despite bilateral obligations, and the sites remain uncomfortable evidence of a past that unsettles national narratives. This paper examines a ‘heritage from below’ response: volunteers who clear, restore and revitalise these dissonant burial grounds. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in cemeteries in the Ústí nad Labem Region (2025–2026) that included interviews with 15 volunteers from seven initiatives caring for nine cemeteries, the paper explores why people choose to care for heritage that local communities associate with guilt, anger and resentment. Volunteers’ aims developed organically from ‘rescue’ towards creating places of remembrance and contemplation. Volunteer labour was sustained by sociability, the satisfaction of physical work, respect for the dead and, among leaders, a sense of reparation and reconciliation. Engaging critically with the concept of ‘heritage from within’, which presumes a biographical attachment to the heritage cared for, the paper argues that the volunteers’ status as outsiders was central to their capacity to engage with, and at times set aside, the dissonance of these sites.

title: Book Review of A History of Economic Thought in France by Gilbert Faccarello and Claire Silvant (eds.)
abstract: A History of Economic Thought in France, edited by Gilbert Faccarello and Claire Silvant, is a two-volume work that brings together a distinguished group of scholars with long-standing expertise in French political economy. The first volume, Political Economy in the Age of Enlightenment, comprises nine chapters and covers the development of economic thought in France from the late 17th century to the eve of the French Revolution. The second volume, The Long Nineteenth Century, continues the narrative across the 19th century, tracing the transformation of economic reasoning amid liberal, formalist, and critical traditions. These volumes offer fresh insights and demonstrate the originality of French contributions to political economy, often neglected or underestimated in Anglophone scholarship. Together, the volumes situate economic ideas within their broader intellectual, political, and cultural contexts.

title: Mauro Boianovsky: An Exemplary Scholar
authors: JHET Assistant, FELIPE ALMEIDA, John Berdell
abstract: This study introduces the late Mauro Boianovsky (1959–2024), one of the most distinguished historians of economics of his generation. Drawing on interviews and correspondence with his colleagues, co-authors, former students, and his sister, the study offers a portrait of his academic trajectory and intellectual contributions. It examines Boianovsky’s connection to Brasília and the University of Brasília (UnB), his training as an economist/historian of economics, and his engagement with colleagues and the broader history of economics community. The study aims to provide a lasting record of a remarkable scholar and to make the significance of Boianovsky’s contributions accessible to future generations. As the introduction to this symposium, it also briefly presents the other papers included in the collection.

title: Book Review of Relocating Development Economics: The First Generation of Modern Indian Economists by Maria Bach
abstract: The product of PhD research at King’s College London, this fine volume discusses the work of the first generation of Indian economists between the last quarter of the nineteenth century and the early twentieth century. Maria Bach’s original question, in her own terms, was to explore “how the first generation of modern Indian economists functioned in a Eurocentric world on their own terms and in what ways they challenged the status quo” (p. 157). Those Early Nationalists, as they came to be collectively known, built on ideas they had absorbed as students in the British imperial university system, to create “original, forward-thinking knowledge on economic development” (p. 3).

title: Book Review of "Otto Neurath in Britain" by Christopher Burke and Ádám Tamás
abstract: Otto Neurath praised the merits of war economy from 1909 and argued for using his visual method in peace propaganda in 1933. He worked as the director of the Soviet IZOSTAT in the early 1930s and developed anti-Soviet visual propaganda for the British Ministry of Information from the late 1930s. He advocated the highbrow philosophy of logical empiricism in Vienna, and built a ground-to-earth, comprehensible anti-culture of visual facts called "Isotype" in London. Based on this, one might think that Neurath was changing sides and world views too frequently, which would, no doubt, make it harder to perceive him as a likeable character. But this is not necessarily the case. This impressive new book, Otto Neurath in Britain, portrays the minutiae of the misadventures of Neurath, and, by doing so, unpacks the apparent contradictions in his many-sided and quite controversial legacy.

title: The “Official opponent”? Wassily Leontief’s Idea of Econometric Methods, and the “Expansion of the Field of Direct Observation”
abstract: Several recent works have explored Wassily Leontief’s distinction between standard econometrics, which he called “indirect statistical inference,” and a “direct induction” he called “direct observation.” These works usually understand Leontief’s direct induction through the lens of input-output analysis. I argue that this is too narrow a perspective. Instead, I show how this distinction stemmed from Leontief’s (1929, 1932a) econometric work, when he developed a statistical technique for determining supply and demand curves. By examining lesser-known published texts by Leontief from this period, as well as unpublished material from the archives, it appears that Leontief’s distinction was in part borrowed from Marschak (1931) when they were both in Germany. Like Marschak, Leontief distinguished between two epistemic strategies: indirect, using data from the marketplace, i.e., price-quantity data; or direct, using specific data separately on buyers (e.g., household surveys) and on sellers (e.g., plant surveys). This result fundamentally revises our understanding of Leontief's view of econometrics.

title: Quantitative, Qualitative, or Mixed Methods: Explicitness, Prevalence, and Interrelationship of Methodological Orientations. An empirical study of sociological research using contextual language modelling and bibliometric analyses
abstract: We apply scientometric techniques and methods of automated content analysis to the question of the quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods orientations prevalent in published sociological research. We consider the methodological orientation of the articles as well as corresponding journal characteristics. In terms of scholarly reception, we examine patterns of mutual citation.
