Our empirical analyses are based on data from the Web of Science Core Collection/Social Science Citation Index. At the same time, we provide a concise introduction to some of the basic procedures of relevant computational techniques. We are particularly interested in productive links between conventional scientometric techniques and recently developed language models.

title: Grandchild care, paid work, and cognitive functioning in later life: Heterogeneity across gender and education among grandparents in Europe
authors: Maria Karlene Shawn Cabaraban, Valeria Bordone, Daniela Weber, Bruno Arpino
abstract: As working lives increasingly overlap with grandparenthood, grandparents may increasingly take on childcare responsibilities alongside paid work. By keeping grandparents mentally and socially engaged, this dual engagement may be cognitively enriching but unequal caregiving demands and educational stratification across gender likely differently shape opportunities and constraints. Drawing on role enhancement and role strain theories, we investigate whether the association between grandchild care provision and cognitive functioning differs between working and retired grandparents, once accounting for gender and education. Using a longitudinal sample of 18,748 grandfathers (N = 69,194) and 22,642 grandmothers (N = 79,702) aged 50-80 from the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), we estimate cross-lagged panel models with individual fixed-effects (CLPM-FE) to examine contemporaneous and lagged associations of grandchild care provision and frequency with cognitive functioning (memory recall and verbal fluency), while mitigating concerns about reverse causality and time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity. Results show that, generally, grandchild care is positively associated with cognitive functioning for both genders but only during retirement and particularly for the higher-educated grandparents. Among working grandmothers, however, findings reveal a more nuanced picture: monthly or less frequent childcare is contemporaneously associated with improved verbal fluency, whereas childcare at both frequencies shows a negative lagged associated with memory recall. Together, these results highlight how the cognitive implications of childcare depend on other responsibilities that grandparents hold and point to the need for policies that support the reconciliation of paid work and family care in later life as these domains increasingly overlap.

title: Foundational Asymmetry and the Federal Consolidation Problem: Somalia in Comparative Perspective
abstract: Federal theory usually assumes that a center exists before the units it decentralizes to, or that sovereign units create a center together at one founding moment. A growing number of post-conflict federations follow neither path: member states are built first, and a central government is rebuilt later and then seeks authority over them. This article theorizes these latecomer-center federations. It argues that their stability depends less on how much authority the center holds than on whether central authority grows through shared-rule institutions. Three concepts specify the argument. Centralization without federal consolidation is the expansion of effective central authority before the procedures that define and constrain it are settled. Foundational asymmetry is the unequal institutional inheritance that units bring into a formally symmetric federation. Constituent compact consciousness is a unit's historically grounded claim to have co-authored the compact and therefore to take part in revising it. From these concepts the article derives four general propositions and a typology that places latecomer-center federations alongside coming-together and holding-together federations. It traces the mechanism in Somalia (1998–2025), where Puntland predates the federal government by fourteen years and the Provisional Constitution itself encodes its prior status, and then compares four latecomer-center federations: Iraqi Kurdistan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sudan before 2011 and Ethiopia. The comparison yields a second finding. Resistance takes a different form at each level of inherited capacity: units with materially established institutions withhold recognition and threaten exit, while units whose capacity rests on a founding claim and on recognition by the center escalate to violence when recognition is withdrawn. The framework explains why formally identical centralizing measures provoke unequal resistance, why procedural disputes escalate into disputes over the federation's authority, and why building a strong center and building a federation are distinct tasks. The comparison also shows that the form resistance takes depends on what the older unit holds: institutions it can withhold, a territory it can leave, or an army it can use.

title: Trinity or Trilemma? How researchers assess publications, data and software
authors: Judith Hartstein, Nathalie Schwichtenberg, Alexander Schniedermann
abstract: Understanding what encourages researchers to (re)use publications, data and software and thereby trusting the output of distant and unknown peers, is essential for envisioning future forms of scholarly communication and developing organizational and technical infrastructures. With a survey among more than 1,700 researchers across disciplines we investigate a) how often researchers across the spectrum of disciplines use the three types of resources, and b) how they make the respective use decisions along ten assessment vectors. We find that resource use and assessment practices stabilize across disciplines in line with the integration of a resource into scientific practice, and that assessment practices fall into the three categories of resource specificity, field specificity and user specificity. We contextualize our findings within the broader discourse on epistemic trust, and we conclude that publications, data and software are always to be considered in reference to their similarities, synergies and diversities when it comes to scientific best practices and infrastructure development.

title: ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT IN EARLY TWENTIETH-CENTURY BRAZIL: FRANCISCO SIMCH’S POLITICAL ECONOMY OF COAL
abstract: Influenced by nineteenth-century German economists, the Brazilian mining engineer, lawyer, and professor of political economy Francisco R. Simch (1877–1937) combined economic theory and policy to argue for the exploration of coal mines in Southern Brazil. His interdisciplinary treatment of the issue aligned environmental conservation and regional development, calling for an investigation into his work as representative of an approach to the interlinkages between environment and development belonging to the history of natural resource and environmental economics. He discussed the regulatory role of government, the importance of railways, the need to create industry-specific quality standards for “national coal” to compete internationally, and benefits in terms of balance of payments as well as of the protection of forests against the industrial use of firewood. The article unveils Simch’s political economy as a set of integrated arguments in favor of a transition into coal as an essential source of energy to the belated but steady drive for industrialization in the country.

title: Peer Review and the Technical Soundness of Research: Evidence from Automated Audits of Political Science Working Papers
abstract: Peer review is meant to select high quality work and make it better. To measure one dimension of quality (“technical soundness”), we develop method-specific checklists and a “universal checklist” derived from the published literature by a transparent, rule-based procedure. We then have a language-model coder apply these checklists to 798 working papers posted from 2020 to 2022 on three preprint servers and to 406 corresponding published versions. A one standard deviation increase in preprint soundness is associated with a 10.3 percentage point increase in publication probability and higher journal placement. For the published/unpublished margin, both the universal and the method-specific checklists predict publication outcomes to a similar degree. A “naive” review by the same model, with no checklist, predicts publication about as well overall and less well for top-three journals, but the checklists catch issues this misses and add further predictive power. Published versions score modestly higher than preprints: 67% score higher at publication, and the mean overall score rises by +0.19 standard deviations. We release the checklists and the auditing system as a tool for authors.

title: Leveraging AmCAT to Validate Democracy Research
authors: Soﬁa Gil-Clavel, Wouter van Atteveldt, Jana Bernhard-Harrer, Johannes B. Gruber, Kasper Welbers, Hajo G. Boomgaarden, Mariken van der Velden
abstract: Validation of text and multimedia data remains a central concern for measurement quality in political and democracy studies. Validation should entail the reporting of performance metrics and the systematic construction of a credible chain of evidence supporting a measurement claim. As validation is more than merely contrasting human and machine annotations, validation must be accompanied by enough evidence, data provenance, documentation, and computational materials for an independent researcher to understand what was validated, against what, under which conditions, and with what limitations. Yet implementing these practices requires considerable time and effort, a burden that currently falls largely on individual researchers. It is here where MEDem AmCAT can help. In this article, we introduce MEDem AmCAT and show how it provides the infrastructure where political and democracy researchers can perform the full validation cycle: measurement assessment, data and provenance documentation, workflow reproducibility, and workflow assessment.

title: Cold Homes, Colder Trust: Does Wartime Infrastructure Deprivation Erode Social Capital?
authors: Ruslana Moskotina, Danyil Karakai, Valentyn Hatsko, Dmytro Andreiev, Kateryna Antonets​
abstract: How does infrastructural deprivation as a form of wartime victimisation relate to civilians’ social capital? Drawing on two-wave panel data from Kyiv residents in winter 2025-2026, amid intensified Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, we examine whether deprivation erodes trust and prosociality through the negative affect it generates. We find deprivation associated with lower interpersonal and political trust via negative affect. For political trust, a direct association also emerges, though not across all specifications. Prosociality, by contrast, relates to deprivation only directly, suggesting a resource-based rather than affective mechanism. The associations are modest, indicating notable resilience of Kyiv’s social fabric.

title: Commerce and Peace in the French Revolution: Rougier-Labergerie’s International Political Economy
abstract: This study examines the political economy of international trade and perpetual peace proposed by the agronomist Jean-Baptiste Rougier-Labergerie under the French Directory. Drawing on Rougier-Labergerie’s treatise on commerce and peace, this article shows how a political economy that was rooted in natural jurisprudence navigated the challenges of subsistence and war through turbulent times that extended beyond the Thermidor. Similar to eighteenth-century intellectuals who witnessed large-scale wars waged with public debt in the name of national interest, Rougier-Labergerie considered the possibility of peace and prosperity to be intricately linked to the question of commercial rivalry between nations. He thereby recognized the pressing need to mitigate—by different means from those deployed by the radicals of Year II—the jealousy of trade that plagued Europe in the 1790s. This examination provides a more nuanced dimension to the established categories in historical inquiries into the international political economy of the revolutionary period.

title: Adam Smith on the “wretched spirit of monopoly” in the East Indies trade
abstract: According to Adam Smith, the “wretched spirit of monopoly” dogged the East Indies trade. The regulations that governed the East Indies trade established legal barriers or restrictions to entry and sustained a mercantile community whose interests were “the opposite to that of the great body of the people”. The East Indies charter conferred a special privilege that shielded the English East India Company from all domestic competition in Asian trade. The East India Company was the complete incarnation of a mercantile system against which Smith had determined to launch “a very violent attack” in Wealth of Nations (Smith 1987, p. 251). Smith’s mistrust of trading bodies like the East India Company was compounded by its having assumed political powers commensurate with the sovereign while still in possession of its monopolistic franchise. Smith’s proposal was, first, to abolish the monopolistic franchise to rid society of “the unfortunate effects of all the regulations of the mercantile system”, and second, reform the East India Company’s administrative duties and functions in the Indian territories. The contention of this paper is that Smith’s call to abolish the East Indies monopoly was inseparable from his appeal for reform of the English East India Company.

title: Housing-welfare trade-off and young people's homeownership
abstract: States were instrumental in driving a homeownership boom in the second half of the 20th century. Yet, scholars have long been startled by an empirical fact that countries with more generous welfare states tend to have lower rates of homeownership. Building on this, various theories have attempted to explain a trade-off between welfare state and homeownership, often with the assumption that countries can either have stronger welfare states or higher homeownership levels. In this paper, using data from EU-SILC 2008-2019 for 21 European countries, we show that this seemingly negative association is mainly due to neglecting the housing status of young people. Most young people living with their parents may live in owner-occupied homes, but they do not formally own a house. And accounting for this fact and measuring homeownership at the individual level virtually eliminates the negative association between welfare state generosity and homeownership. This is mostly because living in parental home is more common among young people in countries with less generous welfare states and with high levels of owner-occupied homes such as Eastern or Southern Europe. Moreover, we also show based on multi-level models that more generous welfare state, in the form of higher minimum income schemes, social insurance and childcare provision, is associated with higher level of independent living among young people, and with higher individual homeownership among the higher earning group. Our findings challenge big trade-off theories and show that welfare states can support homeownership, specifically of young people.

title: Zoning for Votes: How Local Politicians Use Land-Use Regulations for Political Gain
abstract: Across many levels of governments, elected officials engage in opportunistic behavior, through political budget cycles or ‘pork-barrel’ spending. Local politicians, however, have more limited ability to manipulate spending or pass popular policies due to federalist budget constraints and preemption. In the face of these constraints, I argue that local politicians use the tools at their disposal, particularly land-use regulations, treating zoning as pork. Using both lot-level zoning data in New York City and national data on historic districts, I show that land-use changes occur disproportionately on municipal election years. This effect is driven by those with the strongest electoral incentives: politicians up for reelection in competitive districts. Additionally, this zoning political budget cycle is larger for density-restrictions, consistent with anti-density public opinion, and tends to target lots with politically active residents. These findings suggest strategic electoral incentives help explain why many cities have restricted new housing despite an affordability crisis.

title: 500+ Job Applications Later: Reflections on the Economics PhD Job Market
abstract: The economics PhD job market is a highly structured and centralized matching process that aims to reduce search frictions, yet remains intensely competitive, uncertain, and emotionally demanding for candidates. While much of what is known about candidates' experiences comes from personal anecdotes and informal conversations, this paper offers a first-person account of the 2025\textendash 2026 economics PhD job market, supported by descriptive empirical evidence from more than 500 applications across sectors, geographic regions, and institution types. Drawing on my experience as a candidate from a mid-ranked doctoral program, I document application patterns, first-round interview outcomes, and the practical and emotional challenges of navigating the recruitment process. Particular attention is given to less visible aspects of the market, including prolonged uncertainty and silence, limited communication from prospective employers, and the administrative burden of navigating different application systems. Rather than attempting to draw generalizable conclusions from a single candidate's experience, I offer a candid account of the measurable outcomes and personal difficulties of an extended job search. I hope this account provides future candidates with a more realistic understanding of what to expect and reassurance that rejection, uncertainty, and setbacks are common and do not necessarily reflect their abilities or research potential.

title: Better land measures, same output report: GPS area, self-reported production and the inverse size–productivity relationship in Honduran coffee
authors: Carlos de los Rios, José Antonio Mendoza Sánchez, Elena Serfilippi
abstract: We compare the self-reported area of a coffee plot with its area measured by a high-accuracy GPS receiver for 1,443 producers in Honduras, and ask how the land measure affects the inverse size–productivity relationship. Among the 421 producers with a single plot, whose production and area refer to the same land, production rises one-for-one with the declared area (elasticity 0.993) and less than proportionally with the GPS area (0.620). With both measures in the same equation, the GPS coefficient is 0.001 (standard error 0.068): given the declared area, the GPS area adds no detectable information about reported production. This is what correlated errors in self-reported production and self-reported area produce. A better land measure does not give a cleaner test while production remains self-reported.

title: Nocturnal Wayfaring: Walking in the dark
authors: Hannah Dalgleish, Isabel M J Sargent
abstract: How do we find our way in the night? Cities after dark are brighter than ever before, changing how we experience, perceive, and navigate urban spaces at night. Our research asks: how can we come to know the night and our place in it? Through the metaphor of nocturnal wayfaring, we reflect on walking after dark in different nightscapes, alone or together, and from rural to urban environments. We draw upon our own night walks in the port city of Southampton in the South of England, first a reflexive nightnographic walk, and then, a transdisciplinary night walk with local experts. We propose that walking in the dark can be an act of cultivating care and bringing healing to the nighttime city. This work portrays a snapshot in time of a continuously evolving attempt to negotiate the complex narratives and liminal qualities of conducting nocturnal and transdisciplinary research in situ.

title: Digital health interventions in public libraries: a JBI scoping review
authors: Xavier Chan, Tracey Hartness, Rebekkah Curran, Paul Flowers, Megan Crawford
abstract: Background: Digital health interventions offer opportunities to improve healthcare access but may exacerbate existing inequalities through the digital divide. Public libraries provide free access to digital technologies and are embedded within communities, positioning them as potential settings to support equitable access to digital health services. However, their role in facilitating digital health interventions remains under-explored. Objective: To map the existing evidence on digital health interventions delivered or facilitated within public library settings across geographical contexts. Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported using the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Eligible sources included primary research and relevant grey literature published between 2002 and 2025, involving adults and adolescents in public library settings. Evidence was charted and synthesised using descriptive frequency analysis and narrative synthesis. Results: Twelve studies published between 2016 and 2024 were included. Eleven studies were conducted in the United States and one in the United Kingdom. Four categories of digital health interventions were identified: telemedicine (n=6), virtual reality (n=3), digital therapeutics (n=2) and online health education (n=1). Findings highlighted the potential of public libraries to improve access to healthcare, particularly for rural communities and digitally excluded populations. Free access to technology, staff support and trusted community environments facilitated engagement. However, implementation challenges included limited resources, staff capacity, privacy and confidentiality concerns, and mental health stigma. Conclusion: Public libraries represent a promising but underdeveloped setting for facilitating equitable access to digital health interventions. Further research across diverse geographical contexts and intervention types is needed to understand implementation requirements and inform sustainable service development.

title: ‘Neutral’ Ground or Party Ground? Right-Wing Populism and the Subnational Politics of Adult Education in Germany
authors: Renan Sari Winkler, Hung H. V. Nguyen
abstract: As RWPPs become central political actors in local-level policymaking, the question arises if and how this development influences democracy building and integration. Adult education policy is crucial for these domains and is heavily influenced by local-level politics. We expect that RWPPs aim to reduce courses in the fields of civic education, environment, diversity, and integration. Germany is an ideal case to study this phenomenon, and we therefore investigate the impact of the AfD’s rhetorical and electoral strength at the local level on adult education course provision. We use data from the Local Manifesto Project, county-level seat shares, and adult education course provision (2009-2023). Applying an automated, sentiment-based text analysis of local manifestos and estimating within-county models, our findings do not reveal that RWPPs affect course provision in the respective areas systematically. This suggests that political ‘firewalls’ and the institutional resilience of adult education providers continue to restrict RWPPs influence.

title: Saturation Prompting: Recovering Stable Categories from Open-Ended Survey Responses with Repeated LLM Extraction
abstract: A single large language model (LLM) call cannot reliably find the categories in open-ended survey responses because the model samples from a probability distribution and returns different themes each run, so one list cannot tell which belong to the data and which to that draw. The pipeline documented here improves reliability and reproducibility through saturation prompting, in which many independent calls each read a fresh random sample. It counts how often each theme is found and gives a distribution rather than a flat list. For researchers who want a shorter list, the pipeline can also merge labels with the same meaning into a final scheme of distinct categories. To test the pipeline, I apply saturation prompting to four open-ended survey questions from the UC Berkeley Social Networks Study and compare the results with a single call to the same model. Against the study’s existing codebooks, built by hand and independently, Llama 3.1 8B saturation runs recover 43 to 47 of their 50 categories, against 31 to 37 for its single calls, with the gain on the two more interpretive questions; on the two concrete questions a single call already finds most of them. On a more capable model, Claude Sonnet 5, saturation prompting adds less than it does for Llama over a single prompt asking the model to extract as many categories as it can find. Still, for both models and on every question, saturation finds more distinct categories than a single call. Llama’s additions include whole broad categories, while Sonnet’s are mostly more nuanced distinctions within broad categories its single call already finds. Saturation prompting makes a lower-tier open-weight model that can run on a laptop more reproducible by reducing run-to-run variability. Averaged across the four questions, the similarity between two runs’ ten most frequent labels rises from 0.85 for a single call to 0.96 with 64 calls (1.0 = identical meaning). Merging, although convenient, keeps only 33 to 91 percent of the distinct categories a saturation run finds.

title: State cooperation policies and local political geography explain spatial patterns in U.S. immigration enforcement, 2023-2026
authors: Asad L. Asad, David Broska, Gerard Torrats-Espinosa
abstract: Immigration enforcement, which includes arrests of noncitizens in law enforcement custody (``law enforcement arrests'') and those made in the community (``community arrests''), can occur in any U.S. county. Yet some counties experience more of one or both types of immigration enforcement than other counties, and these spatial patterns can vary across presidential administrations. We evaluate two theoretical explanations for these patterns: (1) state cooperation policies that require or circumscribe federal-local collaboration in immigration enforcement, and (2) political geography, whereby immigration enforcement aligns with the ostensible partisan interests of local voters. Drawing on immigration arrest data between December 3, 2023 and August 5, 2026, we examine the patterning of immigration arrests across counties in the second Trump administration relative to the Biden administration. We find that state cooperation policies and political geography both matter for where arrests occur, but they operate under distinct conditions. Relative to the Biden administration, immigration arrests during the Trump administration have increased in most counties, regardless of state cooperation policies. But immigration arrests, particularly law enforcement ones, have increased most where states require rather than limit cooperation. Law enforcement arrests have also increased most where President Trump won a larger share of votes in the 2024 election, regardless of state cooperation policies. By contrast, community arrests have increased most where state policies require federal-local cooperation in immigration enforcement and where President Trump won more votes. Surges in community arrests have been most likely where Vice President Harris received more votes than President Trump, regardless of state cooperation policies. We conclude that, alongside state cooperation policies, political geography may represent an undertheorized explanation for spatial differences in immigration enforcement across presidential administrations.

title: Why We Should Stop Using the Term Gendered Family Violence
abstract: I support ending the use of gendered family violence as the organising description of family violence. Gendered theories and population patterns can inform research and prevention. They cannot by themselves establish who used violence, who experienced it, or why it occurred in an individual family. This analysis examines how gendered framing operates through service eligibility, referral pathways and the ordering of competing inquiries. In Australia, the State of Victoria’s Orange Door and Multi-Agency Risk Assessment and Management (MARAM) materials document differences in service access and assessment pathways. Family Justice Council guidance in England and Wales gives domestic-abuse inquiries priority when considering allegations of alienating behaviour. These jurisdictions and arrangements differ: Victoria provides explicit gender-differentiated pathways; the Family Justice Council guidance prioritises domestic-abuse inquiries, whose relationship to gendered framing requires separate examination. The evidence examined raises questions about whether possible victimisation and perpetration receive equivalent scrutiny across genders. It does not establish the accuracy of every classification or reassessment. Transparent criteria and independent evaluation are needed. The analysis also questions whether the gendered framework adequately accounts for the available research, or gives supportive evidence greater standing than findings that challenge its organising assumptions. Research documents violence in more than one direction, including parental alienating behaviours affecting mothers and fathers. Assessment must examine conduct, context, effects and risk, while distinguishing protective responses from abusive conduct. Removing gendered from the organising description would leave gender-related explanations available wherever supported by evidence. Assessment standards, service pathways, and error correction must also be accountable to that evidence.

title: Assessment Without a Waiting Clock: Language, Learning Needs and Institutional Responsibility for Newly Arrived Pupils in Nordic Schools
abstract: When a newly arrived pupil struggles in the language of schooling, the difficulty may reflect limited opportunities to learn that language, an additional learning need, or both. Schools must act before those explanations can always be separated with confidence. This article examines that uncertainty as a problem of educational policy rather than simply a problem of test selection. Drawing on Nordic policy documents and research on multilingual assessment, inclusion and policy enactment, it argues against using time since arrival as a substitute for professional judgement. A distinction is proposed between three periods that are often blurred in administrative practice: residence in the receiving country, access to meaningful language instruction, and the interval between an identified concern and an educational response. The article develops a revisable assessment approach in which classroom support, evidence gathering and specialist evaluation can proceed together. It considers the consequences for family participation, local discretion, resources and administrative accountability. The proposed approach does not claim to identify disability through multilingual assessment alone, nor does it report original fieldwork. Its contribution is a policy argument: uncertainty about cause should not become uncertainty about whether a school must provide support.
